conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. ___, I'm Dr. ___. I’ll be overseeing your care tonight. You were just transferred from recovery after your bronchoscopy. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’m okay, I guess. My chest feels sore, like a deep ache. Not the worst pain ever, but Tylenol won’t touch it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected after the procedure. You had balloon dilation in your trachea and left main bronchus to open up narrowed areas. We gave you some pain meds already, but I see you usually take 10 mg of oxycodone when it’s bad. Is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 5 mg doesn’t help much. I don’t take it often, but when I do, I need the 10 mg. Is that okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we can give you 10 mg as needed. I’ll order that now. You’re on a trach mask with 35% oxygen, and your breathing looks stable—sats at 98%, no distress. Any shortness of breath or coughing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, breathing’s fine. Just the chest pain and… I’ve been having this stomach ache too, up here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Upper belly pain? Can you describe it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Achy, kind of dull. Started a few weeks ago when I began that new pill—Esbriet. I take it with food like they said. No nausea or diarrhea. I had a bowel movement today, so it’s not constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Esbriet—pirfenidone—can cause stomach upset in some people. Since you’re already on famotidine, we’ll increase it to twice a day to help protect your stomach. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I do feel a bit better after my morning famotidine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We also checked a chest X-ray after your procedure. It shows low lung volumes and a little atelectasis—meaning some small airways are a bit collapsed. That’s common after sedation. We’ll encourage deep breathing and coughing to help open them up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at all. It’s mild and expected. We’ll monitor it, and it should improve as you move around and breathe deeply. No pneumonia or fluid, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. And the procedure—did it go well?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. They dilated the trachea to 12 mm and the left main bronchus to 9 mm. They also removed some pseudomembrane and granulation tissue that can block the airway. That was sent to pathology, but it’s likely related to your chronic inflammation from relapsing polychondritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s why I’ve been having trouble before? The tissue buildup?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your condition causes repeated scarring and narrowing. That’s why you need these periodic dilations. The team felt the procedure was successful with no complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I just hope it lasts longer this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do our best. You’re on your regular home meds, including prednisone. We’re keeping you on 40 mg daily for five days to reduce inflammation after the procedure, then back to your usual 7.5 mg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, I remember from last time—stress dosing if I get sick?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. If you get an infection or fever, you should triple your dose and use the Solu-Cortef injection if you can’t keep pills down. Always carry your steroid card.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I have the injection with me at all times.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m checking in on you. Your labs from this morning show your white blood cell count is a bit high—18.0. That’s likely from the procedure and inflammation, not infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that concerning? Should we do antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. You’re not running a fever, and your breathing is stable. The rise is expected after tissue trauma. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. My chest pain is better today—only took one dose last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. And your stomach pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but not worse. I’ve been taking the famotidine twice a day like you said.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep that on board. The team recommends you follow up as an outpatient to discuss whether to continue Esbriet long-term, given the stomach side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. It’s supposed to help my lungs, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it may slow lung scarring. But we have to balance that with how it affects your stomach. Your pulmonologist will help decide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. You’re looking well. Vital signs are stable—BP 132/81, heart rate 67, oxygen at 100% on 35% trach mask. We think you’re ready to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news. What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your home meds. Take prednisone 40 mg daily for three more days, then switch back to 7.5 mg. Keep taking famotidine twice a day for now, and use oxycodone only if chest pain returns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Esbriet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue it with meals. But schedule a follow-up with your pulmonologist to review how you’re tolerating it. They’ll also check your lung function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And when should I come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Follow up with interventional pulmonology in a few weeks. And if you have worsening breathing, cough up blood, or fever, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You did well. We’ll send all instructions to your father—he’s listed as your contact, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, he’s my healthcare proxy and knows my history well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. He’ll get a call with your discharge plan. Rest well, and take care.
